HM-03.c01: HazMat can hurt people when a package is damaged, leaks, catches fire, or is loaded next to something it reacts with.
Protect containers: **don't use hooks** or any tool that could damage them.
**Cargo tank** = bulk packaging permanently attached to the vehicle; **portable tank** = filled or emptied off the vehicle, then put on one to move.
**Bulk packaging** = one container of more than **119 gallons** for a liquid; a freight container is 64 cubic feet or more.
**Transport index** = a number on some radioactive labels telling how much control the package needs in transit.
HM-03.c02: Before loading or unloading, **set the parking brake** so the vehicle cannot move, and keep HazMat away from heat.
**Never** transport leaking packages; it is **illegal** to move a vehicle with leaking HazMat.
Never smoke around **5** classes: Class 1, Division 2.1, Class 3, Class 4 and Class 5.
Brace containers so they **cannot fall, slide or bounce**, taking extra care with valves and fittings.
During the trip keep packages **closed** and never transfer HazMat between packages; only a **cargo tank** may be emptied on the vehicle.
HM-03.c03: Cargo heater rules cover **3** classes (Class 1, Division 2.1, Class 3) and usually forbid heaters, including **heater/AC units**.
Class 1, Class 4 and Class 5 may **not** be overhang or tailgate loads; they need a **closed cargo space**.
The exception: every package is **fire- and water-resistant** or covered with a fire- and water-resistant tarp.
HM-03.c04: **Turn the engine off** before loading or unloading any explosives, disable cargo heaters, and check for sharp points.
Division 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3 need a floor liner that is **nonmetallic or nonferrous** (no iron, so not stainless steel).
Never use hooks or metal tools, never drop, throw or roll packages, and refuse any that are **damaged, damp or oily-stained**.
Transfer 1.1, 1.2 or 1.3 between vehicles on a public road only in an **emergency**, with red reflectors, flags or electric lanterns set out.
No 1.1 or 1.2 in a combination with a placarded cargo tank, or with 1.1 A, **Yellow III**, 2.3, 6.1, or a DOT Spec 106A/110A tank.
HM-03.c05: Class 4 solids can react with water, heat or air, or by themselves; Class 4 and 5 must be **completely enclosed** or securely covered.
Keep dangerous-when-wet materials **dry**; spontaneously combustible materials need enough **ventilation**.
Hand-load breakable corrosive containers **one by one, right side up**, on an even floor; stack carboys only if lower tiers can bear the weight.
**Nitric acid** is never loaded above any other product; charged batteries ride upright, protected from falling cargo and short circuits.
Corrosive liquids never go next to or above Div. **1.4, 4.1, 4.3**, Class 5 or Div. 2.3 Zone B.
HM-03.c06: Cylinders ride **upright** in racks or boxes (flat floor if no racks); lying down only if the **relief valve is in the vapor space**.
Never carry 2.3 or 6.1 in containers with interconnections; never put **POISON** packages in the cab or sleeper, or with food.
Radioactive packages labeled II or III show a **transport index**; the total in one vehicle must **not exceed 50**.
Radiation passes through nearby packages, so distance matters: a transport index of 1.1 can't be within **2 feet** of people or cargo-space walls.
HM-03.c07: Poison (6.1 or 2.3) may not ride with **food** unless overpacked in an approved way; mouthwash, toothpaste and skin creams are **not food**.
**Cyanides** must not ride with acids or corrosives, which could release hydrocyanic acid, so silver cyanide and **battery acid** can't share a vehicle.
Charged storage batteries must not ride with **Division 1.1**; Class 1 detonating primers not with other explosives unless in authorized packaging.
**Nitric acid** may ride with other materials only if it is **not loaded above** them.
HM-03.c08: A **cargo tank** is permanently attached and **stays on** the vehicle while it is loaded and unloaded.
A **portable tank** is loaded or unloaded **off** the vehicle, then put on a vehicle to be moved.
The most common cargo tanks are **MC306** for liquids and **MC331** for gases.
HM-03.c09: Show the **ID number** (from Column 4) on cargo tanks, portable tanks and other bulk packaging, such as dump trucks.
ID numbers are black, **100 mm (3.9 in)** tall, on orange panels, placards, or a white diamond if no placards are required.
Portable tanks show the owner's or lessee's name and the shipping name on 2 opposite sides: **2-inch** letters over 1,000 gallons, 1-inch under.
Portable tank ID number: **each side and each end** at 1,000 gallons or more, 2 opposite sides under 1,000; keep it visible on the vehicle.
Specification cargo tanks show **retest dates**; IBCs don't need the owner's name or shipping name.
HM-03.c10: A **qualified person** must always watch a cargo tank being loaded or unloaded.
The watcher must be alert, **within 25 feet** with a clear view, know the hazards and emergency procedures, and be authorized and able to move the tank.
Propane and anhydrous ammonia tanks have **special attendance rules**.
**Close all manholes and valves** before moving a tank, no matter how small the amount or how short the distance.
HM-03.c11: Flammable liquids: **turn off the engine** before loading or unloading, unless it is needed to run a pump.
**Ground** the tank before opening the filling hole and keep it grounded until after closing it, to drain static that could ignite vapor.
Compressed gas: keep liquid discharge valves **closed** except when loading and unloading.
With an engine-driven pump, turn the engine off **after the transfer** and **before unhooking** the hose.
Unhook all connections before coupling, uncoupling or moving a cargo tank, and always **chock** uncoupled trailers.
